description: Eid-ul-Adha, Eid-ul-Fitr, Eid-ul-Ghadeer, Ashura, and Greater vs Lesser Jihad explained.
content_html:
Islamic Festivals: Celebration and Commemoration

Islamic festivals mark pivotal moments in the history of Islam and the lives of the prophets. They serve both to celebrate Allah’s blessings and to deepen a Muslim’s understanding of their faith. Some festivals are observed by all Muslims; others are particular to Shi’a practice. The calendar is lunar, so festival dates move earlier each year relative to the Western calendar.

Eid-ul-Adha: The Festival of Sacrifice

Eid-ul-Adha is one of the two major festivals celebrated by all Muslims, both Sunni and Shi’a. It falls on the 10th of Dhul Hijjah, at the end of the Hajj pilgrimage. The festival commemorates the story of the Prophet Ibrahim, who was commanded by Allah to sacrifice his son Isma’il. Just as Ibrahim was about to obey, Allah intervened and provided a ram to sacrifice in Isma’il’s place — a sign of divine mercy and a reward for absolute obedience.

Muslims worldwide mark Eid-ul-Adha by performing a communal prayer in the mosque or an open space, followed by the sacrifice (qurbani) of an animal — typically a sheep, goat, cow or camel. The meat is divided into three portions: one third for the family, one third for friends and neighbours, and one third given to those in need. This act of sharing reflects the Islamic values of generosity, gratitude and care for the community. For Muslims not on Hajj, it is still a major celebration of Ibrahim’s faith.

Eid-ul-Fitr: Ending the Fast

Eid-ul-Fitr is celebrated on the first day of the month of Shawwal, immediately after Ramadan. It is a joyful occasion that marks the successful completion of a month of fasting, prayer and reflection. Muslims begin the day with a communal prayer, wear new or best clothes, give gifts — especially to children — and share meals with family and friends. Before the Eid prayer, Muslims are required to pay Zakat al-Fitr, a special form of charitable giving to ensure that even the poorest members of the community can share in the celebration. Eid-ul-Fitr lasts for one day (though in some cultures celebrations continue over several days).

Key Fact

Eid-ul-Adha (end of Hajj) commemorates Ibrahim’s willingness to sacrifice Isma’il; animal sacrifice and sharing of meat are central. Eid-ul-Fitr (end of Ramadan) celebrates the completion of fasting; communal prayer, Zakat al-Fitr and family celebration are key features. Both are observed by Sunni and Shi’a Muslims worldwide.

Eid-ul-Ghadeer and Ashura: Shi’a Festivals

Two further festivals are observed primarily by Shi’a Muslims. Eid-ul-Ghadeer is celebrated on 18 Dhul Hijjah, three days after Eid-ul-Adha. It commemorates the event at the pool of Ghadir Khumm, where Shi’a Muslims believe the Prophet Muhammad publicly designated his cousin and son-in-law Ali as his rightful successor and leader of the Muslim community (the Imam). Sunni Muslims do not observe this festival, as they do not share the Shi’a belief about Ali’s designated leadership.

Ashura is observed on the 10th of Muharram (the first month of the Islamic calendar) and is the most solemn Shi’a commemoration. It marks the martyrdom of Hussayn ibn Ali, the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad and the third Shi’a Imam, who was killed along with his family and companions at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE. Hussayn refused to pledge allegiance to the Umayyad Caliph Yazid, whom Shi’a Muslims regard as illegitimate. His death is seen as an act of principled martyrdom in defence of justice and Islam.

For Shi’a Muslims, Ashura is the most important date of the year — a day of intense mourning, public processions, lamentation poetry (marthiya), communal prayers, and plays re-enacting the events at Karbala (ta’ziyeh). Many Shi’a communities in Iraq, Iran and beyond hold large-scale commemorations. For Sunni Muslims, Ashura has a different significance — it marks the day Moses and the Israelites were saved from Pharaoh, and many Sunni Muslims observe an optional fast on this day, following the practice of the Prophet Muhammad. This contrast — grief and lamentation for Shi’a, a quieter fast for Sunni — illustrates how the same date can carry very different meanings across the Muslim world.

Jihad: Greater and Lesser

The word Jihad means ‘striving’ or ‘struggle’ in the way of Allah. It is widely misunderstood — it does not simply mean ‘holy war’. Islamic tradition divides Jihad into two distinct categories: Greater (al-jihad al-akbar) and Lesser (al-jihad al-asghar).

The Greater Jihad is the inner, personal struggle against one’s own ego, desires, selfishness, anger and moral failings — striving to live according to “the straight path” (as-sirat al-mustaqim). This is considered the more difficult and more important form of Jihad. A well-known hadith, attributed to the Prophet Muhammad after a military campaign, describes him as saying they had returned from the lesser struggle to the greater struggle — the struggle against the self. This hadith has shaped Islamic spiritual understanding across the centuries. The concepts of Ma’ruf (what is right and good) and Munkar (what is wrong and evil) are central to Greater Jihad: striving for the straight path means actively promoting Ma’ruf and resisting Munkar in oneself and society.

Key Fact

Greater Jihad (al-jihad al-akbar) is the spiritual struggle against the lower self (nafs) — the most important form. Lesser Jihad (al-jihad al-asghar) is the outward, defensive struggle. Islamic tradition is explicit that Greater Jihad takes precedence over Lesser Jihad.

Lesser Jihad and Its Conditions

The Lesser Jihad refers to outward struggle, which in classical Islamic jurisprudence is strictly defensive — it may be waged only when the Muslim community is under attack, when innocent people are being oppressed, or when evil cannot be removed by other means. The Qur’an sets boundaries: “Fight in the cause of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress limits; for Allah loves not transgressors” (Surah 2:190, al-Baqarah). The Qur’an also commands that if an enemy seeks peace, Muslims must accept it: “But if they incline to peace, then incline to it also and put your trust in Allah” (Surah 8:61, al-Anfal).

The mainstream Islamic scholarly tradition (including bodies such as Al-Azhar University) holds that armed Jihad is only ever defensive and subject to strict conditions: it must be declared by legitimate authority, it must be the last resort, civilians and non-combatants must be protected, and it must cease when the enemy seeks peace. A minority of extremist groups have argued that offensive Jihad is justified to spread Islam — a view that is rejected by the vast majority of Muslim scholars and communities worldwide as a distortion of Islamic teaching. Examiners expect students to present both the mainstream position and divergent views, without endorsing any form of political violence.
exam_tip_html: The most common error on Jihad is reducing it to ‘holy war’ — examiners are specifically looking for you to name and distinguish Greater and Lesser Jihad, using the Arabic terms al-jihad al-akbar and al-jihad al-asghar. Always state that Greater Jihad (inner spiritual struggle) takes precedence over Lesser Jihad. For questions on festivals, be precise: Eid-ul-Adha and Eid-ul-Fitr are shared by all Muslims; Eid-ul-Ghadeer and Ashura are Shi’a-specific. For the 15-mark Discuss, you might be asked whether Greater Jihad is more important than Lesser — develop both sides with sources (Surah 2:190 for Lesser Jihad; the hadith tradition for Greater). Accurate spelling of Eid-ul-Adha, Eid-ul-Ghadeer, Ashura, Hussayn and Munkar is rewarded on extended responses.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Eid-ul-Adha (sacrifice, end of Hajj) and Eid-ul-Fitr (end of Ramadan) are shared by all Muslims; Eid-ul-Ghadeer (Ali’s appointment at Ghadir Khumm) and Ashura (martyrdom of Hussayn in 680 CE) are Shi’a festivals.
  • Jihad means striving in the way of Allah: Greater Jihad (al-jihad al-akbar) is the spiritual struggle against the self (nafs) and takes precedence; Lesser Jihad (al-jihad al-asghar) is the outward defensive struggle, tightly constrained by Islamic jurisprudence.
  • Ma’ruf (promoting what is right) and Munkar (forbidding what is wrong) are central to Jihad; Surah 2:190 limits Lesser Jihad to defensive action, and Surah 8:61 requires Muslims to accept peace when offered.

practice_questions.text: State what event Ashura commemorates for Shi'a Muslims.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for: the martyrdom of Hussayn ibn Ali / the death of Hussayn at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE / the martyrdom of the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad. [1 mark]

Two marks for any two of: communal prayer at the mosque or open space / wearing new or best clothes / giving gifts especially to children / sharing meals with family and friends / paying Zakat al-Fitr (special charitable payment before Eid prayer) / the festival marks the successful completion of Ramadan. [2 marks — 1 per valid point]

practice_questions.text: Outline what Muslims mean by 'Greater Jihad'.
practice_questions.marks: Three marks for: Greater Jihad (al-jihad al-akbar) is the inner / spiritual struggle / against the lower self (nafs) / to resist sin, selfishness and moral failing / to live according to 'the straight path' (as-sirat al-mustaqim) / it is considered more important than Lesser Jihad / it involves promoting Ma'ruf (what is right) and resisting Munkar (what is wrong). Award three marks for a developed outline covering at least two of these elements. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two conditions that Islamic teaching places on Lesser Jihad.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Lesser Jihad must be defensive, not offensive. The Qur'an states: 'Fight in the cause of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress limits' (Surah 2:190). This means armed struggle is only permitted when the Muslim community is under attack.
• If the enemy seeks peace, Muslims must accept it. Surah 8:61 teaches: 'if they incline to peace, then incline to it also and put your trust in Allah.' This prevents Jihad from being used as a pretext for endless conflict.
• Lesser Jihad must be declared by legitimate authority and be a last resort when other means of resolving injustice have failed.
• Non-combatants and civilians must be protected — Islamic jurisprudence forbids harming the innocent.
Mastering: Two developed conditions, each supported by a named Qur'anic source, with clear explanation of significance.
Secure: Two conditions developed, at least one source.
Developing: Two conditions but limited development or no source.
Emerging: One condition, brief. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Greater Jihad is more important than Lesser Jihad for Muslims today.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The hadith tradition records Muhammad as telling his companions after a military campaign that they had returned from the lesser struggle to the greater struggle — the struggle against the self. This shows the Prophet himself placed Greater Jihad above Lesser.
• The inner spiritual struggle against sin, selfishness and moral weakness is relevant to every Muslim every day, whereas armed struggle is rarely applicable in most Muslims' lives.
• Greater Jihad (al-jihad al-akbar) — striving to promote Ma'ruf and resist Munkar within oneself — is the foundation of Muslim ethics and shapes daily behaviour continuously.
• In non-Muslim majority countries, Lesser Jihad in the military sense has no direct application for most Muslims; Greater Jihad is universally meaningful.

Arguments against:
• Lesser Jihad is listed as one of the Shi'a Ten Obligatory Acts and is therefore a formal religious duty, not simply optional.
• Some Muslim scholars argue that defending the oppressed and resisting injustice through legitimate means is an urgent communal obligation that cannot be postponed in favour of inner reflection alone.
• The Qur'an does specify conditions under which Lesser Jihad is obligatory (Surah 2:190), suggesting it cannot simply be set aside.
• What counts as 'more important' depends on context: in times of persecution or injustice, some scholars argue external struggle becomes the pressing duty.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed, named sources (hadith tradition, Surah 2:190, Surah 8:61), explicit comparison of individual and communal dimensions, explicit weighing and a justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Both sides developed, at least one source, clear conclusion.
Developing: Some engagement with both sides, limited sources or weak conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided, brief, minimal sources. [15 marks — SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline the origin and significance of Eid-ul-Ghadeer for Shi'a Muslims.
practice_questions.marks: Three marks for: Eid-ul-Ghadeer is celebrated on 18 Dhul Hijjah / it commemorates the event at Ghadir Khumm / where Shi'a Muslims believe the Prophet Muhammad publicly appointed his cousin Ali as his rightful successor and Imam / it reflects the central Shi'a belief in the Imamate (the divinely guided leadership of Ali and his descendants) / it is not celebrated by Sunni Muslims who do not share this belief about Ali's appointment. Award three marks for a developed, accurate outline. [3 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following correctly describes Ashura for Shi'a Muslims?
options: A joyful celebration of the appointment of Muhammad as Prophet
A day of mourning for the martyrdom of Hussayn ibn Ali at Karbala in 680 CE
The festival marking the end of Ramadan
A commemoration of the Hijra from Mecca to Medina

knowledge_checks.q: What does 'Greater Jihad' (al-jihad al-akbar) refer to?
options: A military campaign to defend the Muslim community
The inner spiritual struggle against one's own ego and sins
The obligation to give 20% of earnings to the poor

knowledge_checks.q: Eid-ul-Adha commemorates the willingness of the Prophet _____ to sacrifice his son Isma'il.
In Islamic teaching, _____ refers to what is right and good, while Munkar refers to what is wrong and evil.
Match each festival to its correct description:
right: Celebrates the end of fasting in Ramadan
Marks the sacrifice of Ibrahim and the end of Hajj
Shi'a day of mourning for the martyrdom of Hussayn

flashcard_questions.a: Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son Isma'il in obedience to Allah.

flashcard_questions.q: How is the sacrificed animal's meat divided during Eid-ul-Adha?
flashcard_questions.a: One third to the family, one third to friends and neighbours, one third to the poor.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Eid-ul-Fitr and when does it occur?
flashcard_questions.a: The festival marking the end of Ramadan; celebrated on the first day of Shawwal.

flashcard_questions.q: What special payment is required before the Eid-ul-Fitr prayer?
flashcard_questions.a: Zakat al-Fitr — a charitable payment so the poor can also celebrate Eid.
The appointment of Ali as the Prophet's rightful successor at Ghadir Khumm.
The grandson of Muhammad and the third Shi'a Imam, martyred at Karbala in 680 CE.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Greater Jihad (al-jihad al-akbar)?
flashcard_questions.a: The inner spiritual struggle against the lower self (nafs) to live according to Allah's guidance.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Lesser Jihad (al-jihad al-asghar)?
flashcard_questions.a: The outward, defensive struggle to protect the Muslim community or remove evil from society.

flashcard_questions.q: Which form of Jihad takes precedence in Islamic tradition?
flashcard_questions.a: Greater Jihad — the inner spiritual struggle — takes precedence over Lesser Jihad.
What is right and good in Islamic ethics — Muslims are obligated to promote it.
What is wrong and evil in Islamic ethics — Muslims are obligated to resist and prevent it.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Qur'anic verse limits Lesser Jihad to defensive action?
flashcard_questions.a: Surah 2:190 — 'Fight those who fight you, but do not transgress limits.'

glossary_terms.definition: The Festival of Sacrifice, observed at the end of Hajj; it commemorates the willingness of Ibrahim to sacrifice his son Isma'il in obedience to Allah.
The festival marking the end of Ramadan and the month of fasting; one of the two major celebrations shared by all Muslims.
A Shi'a festival celebrated on 18 Dhul Hijjah, commemorating the event at Ghadir Khumm where Muhammad is believed to have appointed Ali as his rightful successor.
A day of mourning observed primarily by Shi'a Muslims on the 10th of Muharram, commemorating the martyrdom of Hussayn ibn Ali at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE.
The cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad, regarded by Shi'a Muslims as the first rightful Imam and successor to Muhammad.
The grandson of the Prophet Muhammad and the third Shi'a Imam, killed at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE; his death is central to Shi'a devotion.
An Arabic word meaning 'striving' or 'struggle'. In Islam it refers to effort in the way of Allah, divided into the Greater Jihad (spiritual struggle) and the Lesser Jihad (outward struggle).

Al-jihad al-akbar — the inner spiritual struggle to overcome one's lower self (nafs), resist sin and live according to Allah's guidance; regarded in Islamic tradition as the most important form of Jihad.
Al-jihad al-asghar — the outward, defensive struggle to protect the Muslim community or remove evil from society; tightly constrained by classical Islamic jurisprudence.
What is right and good, recognised as such in Islamic ethics; Muslims are obligated to promote it.
What is wrong and evil, rejected in Islamic ethics; Muslims are obligated to resist and prevent it.
